summary: Provides advice on the ifStackTable, an SNMP interface table, for the Point-to-Point interface over a LAN type. RFC 5309 defines the P2P circuit type for link-state routing protocols, and identifying the correct circuit type matters for adjacencies and link monitoring. The guidance helps operational control, maintenance, and statistics. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers sometimes treat a shared cable as a private line between two machines. This explains how to list that setup in the device's inventory table so people read it properly.

questions: how to model p2p over lan in ifstacktable
what is the p2p over lan interface type
how does a p2p interface relate to the physical link
subtitle: How to describe point-to-point links over shared cables in SNMP tables

tldr.problem: Routers sometimes treat a shared cable (like Ethernet) as if it were a private link between two machines (point-to-point), but the standard SNMP interface table (ifStackTable) has no clear way to represent this setup.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5309 defined the P2P circuit type for routing protocols; this RFC assigns ifType 303 (p2pOverLan) as the interface type and provides examples of how to stack it in the SNMP table with routing and link layers above and below it.
tldr.outcome: Network management tools can now automatically discover and report that a link is point-to-point over a physical LAN, allowing routing protocols to inherit the correct mode without manual configuration.

today: RFC 9296 is the current authoritative reference for the p2pOverLan ifType (303) and is used by network management tool vendors and operators implementing P2P circuit detection and management. It does not mandate any changes to existing deployments but provides a standard way to represent P2P links for those who wish to do so.

sections.title: Introduction and P2P over LAN
sections.content:
RFC 5309 defined the Point-to-Point (P2P) circuit type for use in link-state routing protocols like IS-IS. Identifying the correct circuit type matters because it affects how routers form adjacencies, flood link-state database packets, and monitor link state.

In practice, some routers treat a shared LAN link (such as Ethernet) as a point-to-point link in their routing logic. This is useful for dedicated circuits or for treating a link as logically P2P even when the underlying physical medium is shared. However, the standard SNMP interface table had no standard way to represent this arrangement.

This RFC assigns ifType 303 to p2pOverLan and provides guidance on how to use the ifStackTable to define the relationship between the routing layer, the P2P interface, and the physical link layer. The guidance enables management tools to automatically infer the correct circuit type and routing mode without requiring explicit configuration in the routing protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers talk to each other over wires. A wire can be shared (many routers) or private (just two). Sometimes a shared wire acts like a private line. You write this down in the router's table so management tools get it right.

sections.title: The Interface Stack Table Structure
sections.content:
In SNMP and the YANG data model (RFC 8343), each network interface has an entry in the interface table. The ifStackTable (also called the interface stack) defines which layers stack on top of each other.

For a P2P interface over a LAN, the stack has three layers:

Upper layer (higher-layer-if): typically ipForward (ifType 142), the IP routing layer that uses the P2P interface.

P2P interface (middle): p2pOverLan (ifType 303), signaling that this is a point-to-point link.

Lower layer (lower-layer-if): any appropriate link-data layer such as ethernetCsmacd (Ethernet), l2vlan (VLAN), ieee8023adLag (Link Aggregation Group), or other physical or virtual links that can carry IP.

The RFC provides YANG examples showing how to define this stack. A p2pOverLan interface can be independently shut down (disabled) without affecting the underlying physical interface, allowing operators to treat the P2P logical link separately from the physical link for configuration and troubleshooting.
sections.plainLanguage: Layer 1: The physical wire (Ethernet, VLAN, LAG). Layer 2: The P2P claim (this wire is private). Layer 3: IP routing. Write them in order.

sections.title: P2P Interface Statistics and Administrative State
sections.content:
Each interface in the SNMP table has statistics counters (octets in and out, packet counts, errors) and an administrative state (up or down). For a P2P interface over a LAN, the statistics show traffic that the P2P interface carries, which may include traffic from multiple upper-layer interfaces bound to the same physical port.

The key relationship between the P2P interface state and the underlying link is defined as follows: if the P2P interface is administratively up, then its operational status (oper-status) must fully reflect the operational state of the underlying physical link. If the physical link goes down, the P2P interface goes down. If the P2P interface is administratively down, then its operational status is down regardless of the physical link state.

This allows operators to shut down the P2P logical link (disabling routing over it) without disabling the physical link, which might still carry other traffic. The RFC provides examples showing these state transitions and how to represent them in the YANG model.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep track of how much data flows through the P2P link. If you turn off the P2P interface, the link goes dark even if the wire is still working. If the wire breaks, the P2P interface breaks with it.

sections.title: IANA Registration and Reference
sections.content:
IANA previously assigned the value 303 to p2pOverLan in the Interface Types (ifType) registry. This RFC now serves as the reference definition for ifType 303, replacing the previous reference to RFC 5309.

The assignment was made via Expert Review, following the process defined in RFC 8126. The IANA YANG iana-if-type module (originally RFC 7224) has been similarly updated to reference this document as the authoritative source for the p2pOverLan interface type.

This makes RFC 9296 the canonical reference for vendors, operators, and management tool developers implementing or deploying p2pOverLan interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet authority wrote this wire type code (303) in the official list, and now this RFC is the place to look if you need to know what code 303 means.
